newsitem.title: USA: Albright aids Plavsic in war crimes case.
newsitem.headline: Albright aids Plavsic in war crimes case.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright intervened to help free two Bosnian Serbs, including the son of a slain war crimes suspect, who were arrested during NATO's first operation against Bosnia war criminals, the State Department said on Friday.

Albright responded to a request from Biljana Plavsic, the Bosnian Serb president who is battling efforts by hardliners led by indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic to oust her, a department spokesman said.

Albright telephoned Plavsic, whom the United States has strongly supported as an alternative to Karadzic, on Thursday to explain the NATO operation -- the alliance's first move to capture persons indicted for war crimes during the Bosnia war, spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

One man, Simo Drljaca, former police chief of Prijedor in the Bosnian Serb republic, was fatally shot when he took aim at approaching British troops. Another, Milan Kovacevic, director of a Prijedor hospital, was arrested and taken to the international war crimes tribunal at The Hague.
Burns said that in the telephone call, Plavsic expressed concern that during the operation two of Drljaca's relatives, including his 17-year-old son, were also taken into custody.

"And we know that was a particular concern of Mrs. Plavsic and so we, working with the British and others, I think were able to make sure that two relatives of Mr. Drljaca, including his 17-year-old son, were released. And that release was expedited," Burns said.

"We have respect for Mrs. Plavsic ... She faces a lot of political pressure from some of the intransigent dinosaurs in Pale -- you know, some of the criminal associates of Mr. Karadzic -- and I think everybody supports Mrs. Plavsic in her role to maintain the constitutional order in the Republika Srpska," he said.
He noted that Plavsic dissolved the parliament and said "therefore the United States no longer recognises the parliament and will not recognise any act of the parliament."

Burns said the two relatives were probably were detained for "good cause because they were in the vicinity" when NATO troops attempted to arrest Drljaca, but he stressed that "these two individuals were not indicted war criminals."
